title: AI Automation Consulting
outcome: Diagnose a real business process, decide honestly where AI belongs in it, design and validate the automation, and prove what it was worth.

phases.name: Seeing the Process
phases.outcome: Map how work actually flows through an organisation, as opposed to how the org chart says it does.

modules.name: What the Work Involves
modules.objective: Describe what an automation consultant is hired to decide, and what they are accountable for afterwards.
lessons: You are hired for judgement, not for tools
The three engagements: diagnose, design, deliver
Why most automation projects fail on the process, not the technology
What you own when it goes wrong
Working this job at variable capacity
practice: Classify eight client requests by the engagement they actually need
lab: Write your own engagement one-pager
A one-page description of what you do, what you don't, and what a client gets

modules.name: Mapping Work As It Is
modules.objective: Produce a map of a real process accurate enough that the people doing it recognise themselves in it.
lessons: The documented process and the real one are different documents
Following one item all the way through
Handoffs, queues and the waiting nobody measures
Drawing a map people will correct rather than nod at
Exceptions: the 20% that consumes 80% of the effort
practice: Turn seven messy process descriptions into maps
lab: Map a process you actually know, end to end
A process map with timings, handoffs and exception branches, validated by someone who does the work

modules.name: Getting the Truth Out of People
modules.objective: Interview the people doing the work so they tell you what really happens, including the workarounds.
lessons: Why nobody tells the consultant about the spreadsheet
Questions that get a story instead of a summary
Interviewing the person whose job you might automate
Written and async interviews when calls aren't possible
Separating what they said from what you concluded
practice: Rewrite eight leading questions into open ones
lab: Run and write up a process interview
An interview record separating quotes, observations and your own inferences

modules.name: Measuring Before You Change Anything
modules.objective: Establish a baseline solid enough that any later ROI claim can be checked.
lessons: No baseline, no ROI — only a story
Volume, time, error rate, rework: the four numbers
Estimating when the data doesn't exist
The cost of an error, and who currently absorbs it
Baselines that survive a sceptical finance team
practice: Build a baseline from seven incomplete data situations
lab: Baseline a real process with the data actually available
A baseline sheet with sources, assumptions and confidence stated per number

modules.name: Finding Where It Actually Hurts
modules.objective: Identify which part of a process is worth changing, which is merely annoying, and which the client is wrong about.
lessons: The bottleneck is rarely where the complaints are
Frequency times pain: ranking candidates honestly
The step everyone hates that costs almost nothing
Telling a client their stated problem isn't the problem
When the honest answer is "don't automate anything"
practice: Rank the automation candidates in seven mapped processes
lab: Produce a ranked opportunity list for a mapped process
A ranked list with the reasoning, including at least one candidate you rejected and why

phases.name: Where AI Belongs
phases.outcome: Decide, step by step, which parts of a process AI should touch, which need rules, and which need a human.

modules.name: What These Systems Can Actually Do
modules.objective: Describe current AI capability accurately enough to promise only what will actually arrive.
lessons: What a language model does, in terms a client can hold
Classification, extraction, drafting, deciding: four different risk profiles
Accuracy numbers and what they hide
Keeping your capability picture current without chasing announcements
practice: Judge eight vendor capability claims
lab: Test one claimed capability against your own examples
A test record with your examples, the results, and what you'd now promise a client

modules.name: Rules, AI, or a Person
modules.objective: Choose the right mechanism per step — most steps that get automated with AI shouldn't be.
lessons: The deterministic step that never needed a model
Where ambiguity is real and rules genuinely fail
Cost, latency and debuggability as selection criteria
Hybrid steps: rules first, model for the remainder
Steps that must stay human, and how to say why
practice: Assign a mechanism to every step of seven processes
lab: Produce a mechanism map for a full process
A step-by-step mechanism assignment with a written justification per AI step

modules.name: The Judgement You Can't Remove
modules.objective: Identify the decisions where removing the human transfers risk onto someone who didn't agree to carry it.
lessons: Decisions that affect somebody's money, health or record
Accountability that can't be delegated to a system
Automation bias: humans stop checking what's usually right
Designing the human step so it's actually done
practice: Decide human-in-the-loop or not for eight steps
lab: Design the human checkpoints for a risky automation
A checkpoint design stating what the human sees, decides, and how you'd know they really looked

modules.name: The Data You Actually Have
modules.objective: Judge whether the client's data can support the automation being proposed.
lessons: Where the data lives, and what shape it's in
Volume, labelling and the examples you'd need
Personal data: what may leave the building
Data that's wrong in a consistent, invisible way
Retention, deletion, and what a client has promised its users
practice: Assess data readiness for seven proposed automations
lab: Run a data-readiness assessment on a real dataset
An assessment with a go / go-with-conditions / no verdict and the evidence for it

modules.name: Naming the Risk Before You Commit
modules.objective: State what can go wrong, how badly, and who bears it — while the client can still say no.
lessons: The failure mode nobody put in the proposal
Silent failure versus loud failure, and which is worse
Regulated processes and the questions to ask first
Writing risk into a proposal without losing the work
Walking away, and how to do it professionally
practice: Write the risk section for seven proposals
lab: Produce a risk register for a proposed automation
A risk register with likelihood, impact, owner and mitigation per row

phases.name: Designing the Automation
phases.outcome: Turn a decision about where AI belongs into a specified, integrable, operable pipeline.

modules.name: Choosing Tools You Can Defend
modules.objective: Select tools on evidence — cost, exit, support, fit — rather than on category popularity.
lessons: The categories: models, orchestration, RPA, and the existing software
Buy, wire together, or build: choosing honestly
Total cost including the parts nobody quotes
Lock-in and what leaving would cost
Evaluating a vendor in a week
practice: Shortlist tools for seven briefs with a stated criterion
lab: Run a structured tool evaluation against real criteria
A scored comparison with a recommendation and the conditions that would change it

modules.name: Designing the Pipeline
modules.objective: Specify an automation as a sequence of steps with defined inputs, outputs and failure behaviour.
lessons: Drawing the pipeline before choosing anything
What each step receives and guarantees
Queues, batches and things that run overnight
What happens to an item that fails halfway
Designing for the day the model is unavailable
practice: Specify the step contracts for seven pipelines
lab: Specify a full pipeline including its failure paths
A pipeline spec an implementer could build from without asking you a question

modules.name: Prompts as Production Components
modules.objective: Treat the prompt as a versioned, tested component rather than a piece of text someone tweaks.
lessons: The prompt is the business logic now
Structured output the next step can rely on
Examples that pin down the edge cases
Versioning prompts and knowing which one ran
Changing a prompt without breaking what worked
practice: Convert seven ad-hoc prompts into specified components
lab: Build and version a production prompt with a test set
A prompt, its test set, and results before and after one deliberate revision

modules.name: Integration and the Systems Already There
modules.objective: Fit an automation into the systems a client already runs, without a migration nobody agreed to.
lessons: The existing systems are the constraint, not the background
APIs, exports, and the system with neither
Identity, access and whose account it runs as
Writing back: the step that makes it real and dangerous
Keeping the manual path working during rollout
practice: Plan integration for seven awkward system pairs
lab: Design an integration into a system with no API
An integration design with its failure modes and the manual fallback documented

modules.name: Building Something They Can Run Without You
modules.objective: Deliver an automation the client's own people can operate, change and turn off.
lessons: The automation nobody can maintain is a liability
Runbooks written for the person who wasn't in the meetings
Making it obvious when it stops working
Training the operator, not the sponsor
The off switch, and who is allowed to use it
practice: Write runbook entries for seven failure scenarios
lab: Write the complete handover pack for an automation
A handover pack: runbook, owner, monitoring, change process and off switch

phases.name: The Engagement
phases.outcome: Scope, price, communicate and close a piece of consulting work without over-promising.

modules.name: Scoping and Pricing
modules.objective: Turn a vague enquiry into a scoped, priced, bounded piece of work.
lessons: The enquiry that means five different projects
Fixed scope, fixed price, and where each one bites
Pricing for outcome without pricing yourself into a hole
practice: Scope and bound seven vague enquiries
lab: Write a full scope and price for a real brief
A scope document with deliverables, exclusions, assumptions, price and payment points

modules.name: Setting Expectations That Hold
modules.objective: Set expectations early enough that they don't harden into someone's success metric behind your back.
lessons: The number in the sponsor's head that nobody said out loud
Saying what won't happen, before the kickoff
Pilots that prove something rather than impress someone
Demos and the gap between demo and production
Written expectations, referred back to without drama
practice: Rewrite seven over-promises into commitments you can keep
lab: Run a kickoff that surfaces the unstated expectation
A kickoff record naming every expectation you found and how each was resolved

modules.name: Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
modules.objective: Explain capability and limits to a non-technical decision-maker without either hype or condescension.
lessons: Explaining the mechanism in ninety seconds
Saying "it will sometimes be wrong" and still being hired
Writing for the person who forwards your email upward
Handling the executive who read one article
practice: Rewrite seven technical explanations for a sponsor
lab: Write and test a capability briefing on a real reader
A one-page briefing plus what your reader got wrong on the first draft

modules.name: People, Politics and Resistance
modules.objective: Work with the people whose jobs the automation touches, rather than around them.
lessons: The person who knows why the last attempt failed
Sponsors, users and the gap between them
When the politics make the project undeliverable
practice: Diagnose the real objection in eight pieces of pushback
lab: Build a stakeholder map with each party's real interest
A stakeholder map naming each party's stake, fear and what would make them an ally

modules.name: Delivering and Closing
modules.objective: Close an engagement so the work survives your departure and the client can say what they got.
lessons: Acceptance: what "done" means, agreed in writing
The final report nobody has to be walked through
The follow-up that catches the drift
Turning one engagement into a reference
practice: Write acceptance criteria for seven deliverables
lab: Write a closing report for a completed engagement
A closing report: what was done, what it achieved, what's still open, who owns it now

phases.name: Validation, Monitoring and ROI
phases.outcome: Prove an automation works at scale, keep proving it, and show what it was actually worth.

modules.name: Checking Output at Scale
modules.objective: Design checks that catch AI errors in volume, when reading everything is not an option.
lessons: You cannot read ten thousand outputs, so what do you read
Sampling that finds the errors rather than reassures you
Automated checks: format, range, consistency, contradiction
Building a gold set and keeping it honest
Second-model checking, and when it just agrees with itself
practice: Design a validation scheme for seven output types
lab: Build a validation harness with a real gold set
A harness reporting accuracy against a gold set, with the sampling rationale written down

modules.name: Deciding How Wrong Is Acceptable
modules.objective: Set an error threshold with the client, in advance, that reflects what an error actually costs.
lessons: "It has to be perfect" is not a requirement
False positives and false negatives cost different amounts
Setting the threshold with the people who absorb the errors
What happens when it breaches, agreed beforehand
Comparing against the human baseline, not against perfect
practice: Set and justify a threshold for seven automations
lab: Negotiate and document an error budget
An agreed error budget with the cost model behind each number

modules.name: Monitoring and Drift
modules.objective: Notice when an automation that worked at launch has stopped working.
lessons: It worked in the pilot and nobody checked since
Input drift: the data changed and nothing told you
Model and vendor changes under your feet
Who gets the alert, and what they're supposed to do
practice: Diagnose the drift cause in eight degradation reports
lab: Design a monitoring plan a client will actually run
A monitoring plan with metrics, thresholds, owner and response per alert

modules.name: Proving What It Was Worth
modules.objective: Measure the real return of an automation, including the costs that don't appear on an invoice.
lessons: Hours saved is not money saved unless something changed
The costs nobody counts: review, maintenance, exception handling
Attribution: proving your change caused the difference
Quality and risk improvements that resist a number
Reporting a result that came in under the promise
practice: Critique seven ROI claims and rebuild them
lab: Build a defensible ROI case from a real baseline
An ROI model with sources, assumptions, sensitivity and an honest confidence statement

modules.name: Capstone — A Full Engagement
modules.objective: Carry one process from first interview to a proposal, design and validation plan you would send.
lessons: Choosing a process worth the engagement
Diagnosis: map, baseline and opportunity list
Design: mechanism map, pipeline and risk register
The proposal, with its limits stated
practice: Answer seven hostile challenges to your recommendation
lab: Deliver the full engagement pack
A complete pack: process map, baseline, mechanism map, pipeline spec, risk register, validation plan and priced proposal

phases.name: Running a Practice
phases.outcome: Find work, price it, protect yourself contractually, and keep the practice sustainable at variable capacity.

modules.name: Positioning and Finding Work
modules.objective: Describe what you do in a way that reaches the clients who need it and repels the ones who don't.
lessons: Proof when you can't name the client
Saying no to work that will hurt you
practice: Rewrite seven weak positioning statements
lab: Write your positioning and one proof piece
A positioning statement and one published piece of proof

modules.name: Contracts, Liability and Data
modules.objective: Know which contract terms matter in AI work and which will hurt you later.
lessons: The clauses that matter in an AI engagement
Liability when the automation gets something wrong
Data processing terms, in plain language
IP: who owns the prompts and the pipeline
When to get an actual lawyer
practice: Flag the dangerous clause in seven contract extracts
lab: Assemble your own standard terms
A short set of standard terms with a note on why each clause is there

modules.name: The Work You Won't Take
modules.objective: Decide in advance which engagements you refuse, and be able to say why without a speech.
lessons: Automations that quietly harm the people downstream
Decisions about people that shouldn't be automated
The client who wants cover, not advice
practice: Decide take or decline on eight engagements
lab: Write your own engagement red lines
A written set of red lines with the reasoning, and a decline template

modules.name: Engagements That Survive a Missed Week
modules.objective: Structure the work so a bad fortnight doesn't cost you a client.
lessons: Designing deliverables that don't need you present
Buffers that are in the plan rather than in your head
What to tell a client when you can't work this week
Pricing that doesn't punish a slow week
practice: Redesign seven engagements to survive a missed week
lab: Restructure an engagement for variable capacity
A restructured plan with buffers, async deliverables and a written contingency

modules.name: Staying Current Without Drowning
modules.objective: Keep your capability picture accurate on a small, fixed time budget.
lessons: What actually changes, and how often
Sources worth reading and the noise to drop
Testing a new capability in an hour
Updating advice you already gave a client
A quarterly review of your own assumptions
practice: Triage seven weeks of announcements for what matters
lab: Run one quarterly capability review
A review naming what changed, what you tested, and which of your advice it revises
